shorts.title: Compound interest and the rule of 72
shorts.hook_text: How does compound interest actually work?

shots.visual: The desk at night; the lamp flicks on over the open ledger.
shots.on_screen_text: How does compound interest actually work?
shots.voiceover: Compound interest. Everyone says it's magic. It's just maths.

shots.visual: A single seed in dark soil in a glasshouse at night, amber lamp light; a sprout rises and a second sprout grows off the first.
shots.voiceover: Year one, your money earns interest. Year two, the interest earns interest too.

shots.visual: The sprouts become a branching plant, each branch splitting again, the glasshouse filling.
shots.voiceover: Rule of 72: divide seventy-two by your rate and that's roughly how many years to double.

shots.visual: The plant fills the glasshouse to the roof, branches pressed against the glass, lamp light through the leaves.
shots.voiceover: At seven percent, about ten years. At three, about twenty-four. Rate and time are the whole game.

shots.visual: Back to the desk; the mechanical calculator's handle turns once on its own and stops.
shots.voiceover: No product. Just the rule. That's one. Follow for one a day.

shorts.cta: That's one. Follow for one a day.

shorts.title: What 500 companies in one fund means

shots.visual: The desk; the screen glows and a faint cool light spreads over the ledger.
shots.voiceover: An S&P 500 index fund. What are you actually holding?

shots.visual: A vast dark warehouse of identical wooden crates in rows, amber lamps overhead, the camera gliding along an aisle.
shots.voiceover: Roughly five hundred of the biggest companies listed in the United States, in one basket.

shots.visual: A few crates near the front are much larger than the rest, the rows shrinking into the dark behind them.
shots.voiceover: It's weighted by company size, so the biggest few make up a big slice of the basket.

shots.visual: Back to the desk; the ledger page turns itself once.
shots.voiceover: That's what the fund is: the list, not a guess. That's one. Follow for one a day.

shorts.cta: That's one. Follow for one a day.
sources: S&P Dow Jones Indices, 'S&P 500' factsheet https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/indices/equity/sp-500/ (float-adjusted market-cap weighted, ~500 constituents)

shorts.title: How a credit score is calculated
shorts.hook_text: Nobody explained credit scores to me. So.

shots.visual: The desk; the lamp dims slightly and the calculator's dials rotate.
shots.on_screen_text: Nobody explained credit scores to me. So.
shots.voiceover: A credit score is a prediction: will you pay back what you borrow.

shots.visual: A brass balance scale on a dark counter; small weights are added to one pan one at a time, the largest first.
shots.on_screen_text: 35% payment history · 30% how much you use
shots.voiceover: In the US FICO model, paying on time is the biggest weight. Then how much of your available credit you're using.

shots.visual: Three smaller weights are placed on the pan; the scale settles level.
shots.voiceover: Then how long you've had credit, the mix of types, and how much new credit you've just opened.

shots.visual: Back to the desk; the ledger closes gently.
shots.on_screen_text: Source: myFICO. Canada and UK use different models.
shots.voiceover: Other countries weigh it differently, but pay on time and keep balances low shows up everywhere. That's one. Follow for one a day.

shorts.cta: That's one. Follow for one a day.
sources: Equifax Canada and Experian UK describe their own factor lists; do not quote US percentages for them

shorts.title: The first time the AI agent wrote to my database
shorts.hook_text: Today I let an AI write to my database. It worked. Then it didn't.

shots.visual: The desk; the small screen brightens and the cool light pulses once.
shots.on_screen_text: Today I let an AI write to my database.
shots.voiceover: I'm building a life app. Today the AI assistant inside it got permission to save things.

shots.visual: A dark library where a brass pneumatic tube carries a sealed capsule from a reading desk up into a wall of drawers.
shots.camera: slow tilt up following the tube
shots.voiceover: You say 'check off my workout', the model picks a tool, the tool writes one row. Clean.

shots.visual: A second capsule jams in the tube; drawers rattle; one drawer opens on its own.
shots.voiceover: Then I checked: the key I'd given it could read anyone's rows, not just mine.

shots.visual: A small brass key on a chain is swapped for a different one; only one drawer glows now.
shots.on_screen_text: Use the user's key, not the master key
shots.voiceover: Fix: the agent now runs with the user's own login, so the database itself refuses anything that isn't theirs.

shots.visual: Back to the desk; the screen settles to a steady glow.
shots.on_screen_text: Lesson: never trust the model with the master key.
shots.voiceover: Give the AI the least it needs. Let the database say no. That's one. Follow for one a day.

shorts.cta: That's one. Follow for one a day.
sources: Creator's own project: scratch-agent edge function runs with the caller's JWT so Postgres row-level security scopes every read and write (supabase/functions/scratch-agent)

shorts.title: What a 1% fee costs over 20 years

shots.visual: The desk; a single coin on the ledger spins slowly and falls.
shots.voiceover: A one percent fee sounds like nothing. Here's the example the US regulator uses.

shots.visual: Two identical glass jars on a dark shelf fill slowly with sand from above; a small hole in the second jar lets a thin stream out.
shots.voiceover: Same hundred thousand, same four percent return, twenty years. One pays a quarter percent in fees, the other one percent.

shots.visual: The first jar is visibly fuller; a pile of leaked sand sits under the second.
shots.voiceover: Ends at about two hundred and nine thousand versus a hundred and eighty-one. The gap is the fee, compounded.

shots.visual: Back to the desk; the calculator handle cranks once.
shots.on_screen_text: Source: SEC investor bulletin on fees
shots.voiceover: Fees compound too, just against you. That's one. Follow for one a day.

shorts.cta: That's one. Follow for one a day.
sources: US SEC Office of Investor Education, 'Updated Investor Bulletin: How Fees and Expenses Affect Your Investment Portfolio' https://www.sec.gov/investor/alerts/ib_fees_expenses.pdf ($100,000, 4% return, 20 years: 0.25% fee → $208,815; 1% fee → $180,611)

shorts.title: What a GPU does that a CPU can't
shorts.hook_text: What a GPU does in 30 seconds.

shots.visual: The desk; the screen's cool light brightens and faint fan noise lines ripple the coffee.
shots.on_screen_text: What a GPU does in 30 seconds.
shots.voiceover: Why does every AI company want graphics cards? Because of how they count.

shots.visual: A single master clockmaker's bench with one brilliant worker at one brass lamp, working fast on one intricate piece.
shots.on_screen_text: CPU: a few very fast workers
shots.voiceover: A CPU is a handful of brilliant workers. Each does complicated things, one after another, very fast.

shots.visual: A vast dark hall of thousands of identical small benches, each with a tiny lamp, all stamping the same simple shape in unison.
shots.camera: slow pull back revealing the scale
shots.on_screen_text: GPU: thousands of simple workers at once
shots.voiceover: A GPU is thousands of simple workers doing the same small sum at the same time. Pixels, and the matrix maths behind AI, are exactly that.

shots.visual: Back to the desk; the screen glow steadies.
shots.on_screen_text: e.g. 16,896 cores on one data-centre GPU (NVIDIA H100)
shots.voiceover: One data-centre chip has nearly seventeen thousand of those workers. That's one. Follow for one a day.

shorts.cta: That's one. Follow for one a day.
sources: NVIDIA H100 datasheet: 16,896 FP32 CUDA cores (SXM) https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/
General CPU vs GPU explanation: NVIDIA blog 'What's the Difference Between a CPU and a GPU?'

shorts.title: Where the 50/30/20 rule came from

shots.visual: The desk; the ledger page shows three ruled columns of different widths (no legible text).
shots.voiceover: Fifty, thirty, twenty. Every budgeting app repeats it. It has an author.

shots.visual: A 2000s-era kitchen table at night with a stack of hardback books and a reading lamp; one book lies open.
shots.voiceover: It comes from a 2005 book, All Your Worth, by Elizabeth Warren and her daughter Amelia Warren Tyagi.

shots.visual: Three glass jars on the table filling from a single jug: a large one, a medium one, a small one.
shots.voiceover: Half of take-home pay to must-haves, thirty percent to wants, twenty to savings and paying down debt.

shots.visual: Back to the desk; the three ledger columns catch the lamp light.
shots.on_screen_text: A guideline, not a law. Source: All Your Worth (2005)
shots.voiceover: It's a rule of thumb for a normal income, not a law. Now you know who wrote it. That's one. Follow for one a day.

shorts.cta: That's one. Follow for one a day.
sources: Elizabeth Warren and Amelia Warren Tyagi, 'All Your Worth: The Ultimate Lifetime Money Plan' (Free Press, 2005), the 50/30/20 'balanced money formula'
